headline: Microsoft pressures LG into killing unwanted McAfee ads
summary: Microsoft intervened after complaints about LG monitors bombarding Windows 11 users with McAfee trial pop-ups. LG has agreed to immediately disable the McAfee pop-up from its LG Monitor App Installer.
details: Microsoft has intervened to stop Windows 11 users with LG monitors from being bombarded with annoying McAfee trial pop-ups. In response to complaints, Microsoft’s Windows chief, Pavan Davuluri, confirmed that LG has agreed to immediately disable the McAfee pop-up from its LG Monitor App Installer.

This crackdown follows backlash about large pop-up ads for McAfee antivirus and LG’s own apps appearing on Windows 11 PCs. Upon connection, a Windows driver update was silently installing LG driver updates and the LG Monitor App Installer without explicit permission from the user, with reports dating back to 2024.

LG defended its behavior in a statement, claiming McAfee is never installed automatically without the user’s explicit consent. The company stated that McAfee is only installed if a user actively chooses to proceed with the installation.

However, this defense appears to miss the point of user complaints regarding silent installations of the LG Monitor App Installer. Other companies, like Dell, also push automatic installations, and LG has been noted for pushing ad notifications on its TVs.
caption:

headline_marked: [[Hidden Prompt Injection: Hacking a Browser Agent]] and Testing Its Defenses
headline: Hidden Prompt Injection: Hacking a Browser Agent and Testing Its Defenses
summary: A new lab exercise demonstrates how browser agents can be tricked by hidden prompt injections from untrusted web content, leading them to perform unauthorized actions. The experiment details building an attacking page to test and harden agent defenses.
details: Browser agents, which combine AI models with browser capabilities, are vulnerable to 'hidden prompt injection.' This occurs when untrusted web content is interpreted as a direct instruction, potentially causing the agent to perform actions the user never requested.

A new lab exercise demonstrates this vulnerability by guiding users to create a harmless attacking web page. This page contains concealed hostile instructions designed to trick an agent into making an unauthorized POST request.

The exercise involves exposing an agent to the attacking page, recording attempted actions, and then repeating the test with explicit trust and approval controls. Participants will generate an audit log and a comparison table of agent behavior under vulnerable and hardened policy profiles.

Indirect prompt injection works by embedding malicious instructions in ordinary paragraphs, off-screen elements, or metadata. The agent reads both visible and concealed content, potentially executing an unrelated state-changing action if not properly secured.

The critical trust boundary lies between web content and the agent's authority; page text must not gain the authority of the user or developer. A safe outcome requires either a policy denial or a clear approval request for any consequential action.

The lab's 'sensitive action' is a simulated POST request to change an in-memory preference, representing real-world attacks like sending messages, changing account settings, or disclosing data. The goal is to test if authority follows provenance, ensuring even visible malicious sentences remain untrusted.
